content: Sorbic acid, also known as 2,4-hexadienoic acid, is a naturally occurring organic compound that is widely utilized as a food preservative. Its chemical formula is C6H8O2. The compound was originally isolated from the unripe berries of the rowan tree (Sorbus aucuparia), which is the origin of its name. Sorbic acid and its mineral salts, such as sodium sorbate, potassium sorbate, and calcium sorbate, are effective antimicrobial agents. These compounds are commonly employed in the food and beverage industry to inhibit the growth of molds, yeasts, and fungi. Among these, the salt forms are generally preferred over the acid form due to their higher solubility in water. When sorbate salts are added to food products, they can cause a slight increase in the pH of the food. As a result, it may be necessary to adjust the pH to ensure the safety and stability of the product. It is important to note that sorbic acid should not be confused with other chemically unrelated food additives that have similar names, such as sorbitol, polysorbate, and ascorbic acid (commonly known as Vitamin C). The European Union has assigned specific E numbers to sorbic acid and its salts for regulatory purposes: E200: Sorbic acid E201: Sodium sorbate E202: Potassium sorbate E203: Calcium sorbate Certain molds, particularly some strains of Trichoderma and Penicillium, as well as some yeasts, have the ability to detoxify sorbates through decarboxylation. This process results in the production of trans-1,3-pentadiene, a compound that emits a characteristic odor reminiscent of kerosene or petroleum. Other detoxification reactions include the reduction of sorbic acid to 4-hexenol and 4-hexenoic acid.
